The French called this time of day “l’heure bleue.” To the English it was “the gloaming.” The very word “gloaming” reverberates, echoes— the gloaming, the glimmer, the glitter, the glisten, the glamour—carrying in its consonants the images of houses shuttering, gardens darkening, grass-lined rivers slipping through the shadows. 

---

During the blue nights you think the end of day will never come.

---

As the blue nights draw to a close (and they will, and they do) you experience an actual chill, an apprehension of illness, at the moment you first notice: the blue light is going, the days are already shortening, the summer is gone.

Sofiya V codes, deejays, and produces various events in New York City.

When I emerge from the black unawareness that I was previously in, I see
that I am at some kind of sinister discotheque. Plush carpeting tugs
unpleasantly at my rubber shoe soles. Large spots of light rotate around the
room and reveal harlequin patterned stained glass clerestory windows. I feel
relief when I recognize some acquaintances in the crowd of partygoers. But
when I rest my gaze on any one person's features, they contort into
something strange and unfriendly.

I try to ground myself in the facts of the space—size,
shape, location, purpose—but it's hard to get oriented in my nauseous
state. The room is big and then it’s small until it’s big once more. No one
at this eerie fête acknowledges my presence, not even in passing glances.
They are dancing automatons whose source of movement is unclear.
Intermittently, I hear a cacophony of small, shrill jingles. Though everyone
is dressed in a range of styles, I notice their shoes are all elongated at
the front with the toe curving up and back towards the ankle. The sound I
hear must be the gleaming silver bells fixed to these pointed toes. I look
down sheepishly at my tattered round-toe combat boots. The taste of metal
blooms unpleasantly in my mouth.

Eventually my unease gives brief way to a rapturous glimmer that
I've never felt before. There is something beautiful in the danger of this
gathering, like a radioactive glow. Or maybe the danger was all in my head.
Perhaps it was my own provincial biases that distorted my fellow dancers'
faces into grotesque masks! Now my heart is soft and open like an oyster! I
close my eyes and start to spin along with the bokeh lights. I enjoy myself until my nausea returns.

My dancing begins to feel compulsive. My spirit becomes small and impotent,
but aware, within my body. Despite the terror, I remain somewhat pleased that I am finally participating.

After an undeterminable period of time, the disco ball reflections
fade, and the harlequin windows begin to glow in warm, technicolor hues of scarlet,
yellow, magenta, and cerulean. The sun must have risen. This realization brings
a sinking feeling to my stomach. I feel dancing bodies pushing into me.

In trying to find the impetus behind the developing stampede, I
notice that the center of the dance floor is collapsing and everything in sight is
being pulled into a whirlpool. Light from various sources bends impossibly towards
the newly formed void. The scattered haze that filled the room earlier is now
a dense river of fog rushing past us. My chest cannot expand against the bassline,
and the flares in my vision multiply and swell until I cannot see at all. I no
longer feel carpet under my boots.

A gentle afternoon light nudges my eyes open. It must be Sunday.
I see faint, multicolor rhombic forms drifting across the drywall of my bedroom
ceiling. Despite the optimism of the vibrant autumn day and an empty to-do list,
I am disturbed by an ambient sense of doom and a metallic echo in my mouth.

An echoing underpass, graffiti declaring that property is theft. Up the steps, and I catch the eye of a student coming out of a laundromat, 
where in the dusk a bill-changer blinks like a red eye. The cold light of a sodium streetlamp illuminates a vacant lot.  
In the distance, the platform of a commuter train station is visible. It is deserted.

In the carriage, my fellow passengers: a balding man in a tracksuit jacket and khaki pants, talking to himself, 
a cluster of teenagers filling the whole carriage with the smell of cheap perfume, a neatly groomed yuppie, smartly dressed, 
staring into his phone, two friends coming back from a hen party, clearly tipsy, loudly discussing people they know.

The train runs for a long time and makes many stops. A brightly lit industrial site drifts past, the outlines of its machinery resembling a fantastical city. The railway company's jingle, playing at every station and warping in pitch as the train quickly pulls away, accompanies the journey. 
The rumble of the rails, the creak of the old carriage. The bored train driver makes long-winded announcements with too much information.

That mural wasn't on that building the last time I was here.

In the train window, streets and buildings that have no counterpart outside are reflected, as if another city were keeping pace with ours tacitly. 
Along those streets move people who seem unable to see the ones beyond the glass. They are dressed plainly enough, yet each of them wears the left shoe on the right foot and the right on the left. Every time I exhale, they glance around uncertainly, as if they have heard something.

At the station exit there is a fast-food place selling food that never quiets hunger. At the bus stops, two timetables hang side by side. 
Somehow every passerby knows, without hesitation, which one is meant for them. My phone connects automatically to a mobile network whose name I recognize, though it is written in a script I have never encountered before.
